title: ASME Stamp Audit NDE Support in Milwaukee, WI
description: Milwaukee vessel, sanitary-tank and boiler repair shops: Level III preparation of the NDE side of your ASME or R review. Ask us for a gap review of your file.
h1: ASME Certification Audit Support in Milwaukee, Wisconsin: NDE for Stainless, Sanitary and Steel Code Shops
html:
In Milwaukee and the surrounding counties, a Code shop is as likely to be welding polished stainless for a dairy or brewery as carbon steel for a boiler room. Whichever it is, the ASME review will test whether your NDE controls match the materials you actually weld. Atlantis NDT, an ASNT NDT Level III consulting company, prepares that part of your quality control system for a new or renewed Certificate of Authorization or a National Board R certificate: written practice, Section V procedures, examiner files, lab controls and records. Tell us what you build and when you are reviewed; we reply within one business day.

What southeastern Wisconsin builds under pressure

Milwaukee's manufacturing base is broad: machinery and engines, foundry and forge work, electrical equipment, and a long food and beverage tradition that runs from the city's breweries to the dairy processors across the state. Wisconsin is also a paper state, and its mills keep boilers, digesters and recovery equipment under constant repair. Pressure-equipment shops in the region tend to serve one or more of these customers:

  • Food, dairy and beverage processors, which buy stainless jacketed tanks, pasteurizer and evaporator components, CIP vessels and air and gas receivers, often built to Section VIII Division 1 with sanitary finish requirements on top.
  • Industrial and institutional steam users, which need boiler repairs, deaerators, blowdown tanks and power piping under B31.1, and expect an R certificate holder for welded repairs.
  • Machinery and equipment builders, which put small vessels, accumulators and receivers inside the products they sell, sometimes in volumes large enough to justify a dedicated vessel line.
  • Paper and process plants, which buy carbon and stainless vessels, heat exchanger repairs and alterations when equipment is re-rated.

That spread matters for the NDE program because it puts austenitic stainless steel, carbon steel and castings through the same shop, and each behaves differently under examination.

Two jurisdictions: the State of Wisconsin and the City of Milwaukee

Wisconsin regulates boilers and pressure vessels through the Department of Safety and Professional Services, Division of Industry Services, under a chief boiler inspector, with the technical rules in chapter SPS 341 of the Wisconsin Administrative Code. The City of Milwaukee, through its Department of Neighborhood Services, is a member jurisdiction of the National Board in its own right. The National Board's synopsis of state laws shows the city adopting the state code and certificates being issued by the State of Wisconsin, so the technical rules are the same, but a shop inside city limits should ask its Authorized Inspection Agency which jurisdiction will take part in its review. The city's published fee schedule lists quality control manual reviews among its services.

Points from the state program that touch a Code shop directly:

  • Installation registration. The installing contractor registers each boiler or pressure vessel installation with the state on the department's form. If you also install what you build, the registration and your data report have to agree.
  • Repairs and alterations. Repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code and are done by a valid R certificate holder. Every repair, routine ones included, is registered with the National Board on the appropriate form under SPS 341.62.
  • Power piping. SPS 341 adopts ASME B31.1 as the power piping standard, so steam and condensate piping on boiler jobs follows B31.1 examination rules.
  • Permits to operate. Power boilers get an annual internal inspection; heating boilers and most pressure vessels are inspected every three years. Inspectors hold a department credential, and National Board commission examinations are scheduled through the department's Waukesha office.

Confirm the current edition and any rule changes with the chief boiler inspector's office before you finalize your manual revision.

Stainless and sanitary vessels: where the NDE program changes

Austenitic stainless steel is not ferromagnetic, so magnetic particle testing, the workhorse of a carbon-steel shop, does not apply to it. Surface examination of stainless welds falls to liquid penetrant and visual examination, and that shifts the weight of a review onto the penetrant procedure and the people running it. Points a reviewer or a careful Authorized Inspector may raise in a sanitary-vessel shop:

  • Contaminant control. Section V Article 6 requires penetrant materials used on austenitic and duplex stainless steels and titanium to be checked for halogen content (chlorine and fluorine), and those used on nickel-base alloys for sulfur. Your procedure should name the requirement, and your consumable records should show certified batches.
  • Post-cleaning. Penetrant residue on a product-contact surface is a contamination problem for your customer. The procedure should say how the surface is cleaned after examination and who confirms it.
  • Finish and examination order. Sanitary finish requirements, often written to customer or 3-A expectations, can lead shops to polish before examination. Polishing can smear metal over fine surface openings, so the sequence of grinding, examination and final finishing should be written down and followed.
  • Volumetric examination of thin stainless. Radiography of thin-wall stainless joints is common and usually bought in. Ultrasonic examination of austenitic welds is harder: coarse grains and beam skewing make standard carbon-steel techniques unreliable, so any UT on stainless needs a procedure developed and demonstrated for that material.
  • Visual examination. Many sanitary welds are judged visually inside and out, including the root side of autogenous tube welds. A Section V Article 9 procedure with lighting, access and borescope rules makes that examination defensible.

Small vessels built inside equipment often fall under the UM designator, which carries its own inspection arrangements; the NDE rules of Division 1 still apply to their welds, and your manual should say how examinations on UM work are recorded.

Castings, forgings and heavy carbon steel

Milwaukee's foundry and machinery heritage brings castings and forgings into pressure work more often than in many regions. Under Section VIII Division 1, a designer can only take credit for a higher casting quality factor when the casting receives the examinations UG-24 lists, and forgings may carry examination requirements in their material specification or in the purchase order. If your shop machines or welds cast valve bodies, flanges or heads into a vessel, the NDE program should cover how those examinations are specified, who performs them, and how the records reach the data report. Magnetic particle testing to Article 7 is the routine surface method on carbon steel, and ultrasonic examination of thick plate and welds follows Article 4.

Winter, unheated bays and examination conditions

A Milwaukee shop does a share of its examinations in cold conditions: in unheated bays during January, on equipment brought in from outdoor storage, or at customer sites in winter. Cold affects several methods at once. Penetrant dwell behavior changes as temperature drops, and once the part is colder than Article 6's standard range allows, the penetrant procedure needs a separate qualification for that lower temperature. Ultrasonic couplant thickens, and sound velocity in steel shifts slightly with temperature, which matters for thickness readings. Condensation forms when cold steel meets warm air, which is bad news for both penetrant and wet magnetic particle work. A reviewer who finds a January examination in your job file may ask how the procedure handled the temperature, so record part temperature on reports where your procedure sets limits.

What the review team will want on the NDE side

An ASME joint review begins with the team studying your quality control manual and continues at your facility, where you show the manual working on Code work or on a mock-up made for the review. The demonstration has to suit the designators you request. For a sanitary-vessel shop, a sensible demonstration item includes a stainless butt weld that needs radiography, nozzle and attachment welds examined by penetrant, and a visual examination with documented acceptance. For a carbon-steel boiler repair shop, the item looks very different, so plan it with your Authorized Inspector.

The NDE questions follow a familiar pattern. Is there a written practice that covers every method you perform, in the edition your Code edition references? Are the procedures Level III approved and available where examiners work? Are outside examiners accepted through a documented step? Are the subcontractor's procedure and personnel qualifications on hand at your facility, as ASME's guidance expects for bought-in NDE? Has someone in your company reviewed each outside report before the Authorized Inspector saw it? Do calibration records cover every instrument used on Code work? For a renewal, the team can ask for the NDE behind any job on your Code work list.

Findings that come up most in shops with this profile:

  • Penetrant consumables in use on stainless without halogen certification on file.
  • A procedure written for carbon-steel UT applied to an austenitic weld.
  • Visual acceptance of sanitary welds recorded as "OK" with no reference to the acceptance criteria.
  • Casting examinations required for a quality factor but missing from the job file.
  • Examiners certified under one written practice edition while the manual cites another.
  • Repair registrations sent to the National Board without the NDE records that support them.

How Atlantis supports Milwaukee shops

Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad. Work for Wisconsin shops combines remote document review with site visits planned around your production schedule. A typical engagement covers:

  • A gap review of the NDE chapters of your QC manual against the Code edition in force, the Wisconsin rules and your customers' specifications.
  • Revision of the written practice, including the rules for accepting outside examiners and for methods your shop performs only occasionally.
  • Penetrant, visual, magnetic particle and ultrasonic procedures to Section V, including stainless-specific penetrant controls and a UT procedure for austenitic welds where you need one, through our procedure development service.
  • Preparation for any procedure demonstration your Authorized Inspector asks to witness.
  • Audits of examiner files, including vision records, training and experience, and Level III examinations under your written practice when you need them. Certification remains your company's act.
  • A mock implementation on your demonstration item and help closing findings afterwards.

The founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, carries ASNT NDT Level III certification in penetrant, ultrasonic, radiographic, visual and magnetic particle testing, and more than 11 years of field experience on international projects. For examiner training before certification, see NDT training in Milwaukee; if you need examinations performed rather than audit preparation, see penetrant testing in Milwaukee and visual testing in Milwaukee.

The responsibilities Atlantis leaves with you

Your company owns the certificate, the quality control system and the decision about what goes into the manual. Your company certifies its examiners under its written practice. The ASME team, your Authorized Inspection Agency and any jurisdictional representative judge the system, and the certificate decision belongs to ASME. Atlantis takes none of those roles. We sit on your side of the table as advisers, with no inspection-agency, review-team or certifying authority of our own.

Radiographs for your Code jobs come from a licensed radiography company. Atlantis does no radiography in the United States, though as a Level III it can review the images, techniques and reports your lab produces. Welding is likewise outside our work: WPS, PQR and welder qualification under Section IX are owned by your welding engineer, and the WPS, PQR and WPQ explainer describes that program. Nuclear construction is not something we support in any form.

Milwaukee readiness checklist

  • Penetrant procedures for stainless and nickel alloys name the contaminant limits, and certified batch records for every penetrant, developer and remover in use are on file.
  • The sequence of grinding, examination and final polishing on sanitary welds is written down and followed.
  • Any ultrasonic examination of austenitic welds uses a procedure developed and demonstrated for that material.
  • Visual acceptance on sanitary and stainless welds references the acceptance criteria, not just a tick box.
  • Casting and forging examinations needed for quality factors or purchase orders are planned at contract review and recorded.
  • Reports record part temperature wherever your procedures set temperature limits.
  • Each outside NDE company has a file in your office with its written practice, certifications, reviewed procedures and calibration evidence.
  • One edition of SNT-TC-1A (or CP-189, if that is your standard) appears in every document that names it, from the manual down to individual procedures.
  • Installation registrations, R-form repair registrations and data reports agree with the NDE records behind them.
  • Your demonstration item exercises the methods you actually use, which for many Milwaukee shops means penetrant and visual more than magnetic particle.
  • Your quality manager knows whether the State of Wisconsin or the City of Milwaukee will be represented at the review.

What to send us to begin

Please send the NDE chapters of your quality control manual, your written practice, the list of procedures with revision letters, certification files for three examiners, your subcontractor files for each NDE company, the calibration register and one finished job package, ideally a stainless vessel that carried radiography and penetrant examination. For a renewal, add your draft Code work list. We return a written gap report, draft corrections for your approval, visit for a mock implementation and stay available through the review. The national ASME audit Level III support page explains the certification process, and the NBIC R-stamp NDE audit support page covers repair certificates. For how we organize audit evidence, see NDT audit documentation.

faq.q: Is the City of Milwaukee or the State of Wisconsin our jurisdiction?
faq.a: Both are National Board member jurisdictions. The city adopts the state code, and certificates are issued by the state, but a shop inside city limits should ask its Authorized Inspection Agency which jurisdiction will take part in the review.

faq.q: Why can't we use magnetic particle testing on our stainless tanks?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless steel is not ferromagnetic, so it cannot be magnetized for MT. Surface examination of those welds relies on liquid penetrant and visual examination, which is why the penetrant procedure gets so much attention in a sanitary-vessel shop.

faq.q: What does Section V require of penetrant materials used on stainless?
faq.a: Article 6 requires halogen content control for penetrant materials used on austenitic and duplex stainless steels and titanium, and sulfur control for nickel-base alloys. Keep certified batch records and make sure the procedure cites the requirement.

faq.q: Our customer wants a mirror finish. Should we examine before or after polishing?
faq.a: Write the sequence down and examine before any finishing step that could smear metal over surface openings. The exact order depends on your procedure and the acceptance criteria, which is a good topic for a procedure review.

faq.q: Can a carbon-steel UT procedure be used on a stainless weld?
faq.a: Usually not reliably. Austenitic welds have coarse grains that scatter and bend the sound beam, so the technique has to be developed and demonstrated for the material. Our procedure development service can write one.

faq.q: Do Wisconsin repairs need to be registered even when they are routine?
faq.a: The state program says repairs, including routine ones, are registered with the National Board on the appropriate form under SPS 341.62, and repairs and alterations are done by an R certificate holder following the NBIC.

faq.q: Can Atlantis serve as our outside Level III?
faq.a: Yes. When your written practice allows an outside agency Level III, we can cover ultrasonic, radiographic, magnetic particle, penetrant and visual methods: approving procedures, examining candidates and reviewing results, while certification stays with your company. See Level III consulting.

faq.q: Will Atlantis shoot the radiographs for our stainless butt welds?
faq.a: No. Radiography in the United States is done by licensed radiography companies, and Atlantis is not one. We can review the radiographs and the technique as a Level III.

faq.q: Does Atlantis write welding procedures for sanitary tube welding?
faq.a: No. Procedure and welder qualification for sanitary tube welding, orbital or manual, is your welding engineer's program, and it is outside the work Atlantis does.

faq.q: Can the gap review be done without a site visit?
faq.a: The document review and the gap report can be. Coming to Milwaukee lets us rehearse the implementation on your actual demonstration piece and sit with your examiners and quality staff over the files, and that hands-on session is where most practical gaps surface.
